$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y(t)) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x(t))-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
J(0,0)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}
at ${x}^{∗}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) & \pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & \pi (0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & 2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5 \\ {y}^{2}-x+4y+4\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=2x+y-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=x+3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=2y+4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+y-2 & x+3 \\ -1 & 2y+4\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(1)+(-1)-2 & 1+3 \\ -1 & 2(-1)+4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}].
$$

\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x & 2 \\ -3 & 2y\end{aligned}].

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(0) & 2 \\ -3 & 2(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}].

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x \\ 2x+3y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2x+1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)=2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+3y)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+1 & 2y \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get 

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(0)+1 & 2(0) \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalue of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=1,\text{ }3.$

Finally, since we both have two real and positive eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{source}.$

$$

$\,$

{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y \\ 1-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & 1 \\ -2x & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & 1 \\ -2(1) & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda \cdot (-1-\lambda )-1\cdot (-2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}.$

Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$
